client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. My team is already short-staffed, and then out of nowhere they assigned me this massive project with a deadline that honestly feels impossible to meet. I don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the work still has to get done.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and that feeling of being overwhelmed when demands keep piling up is completely understandable. You're right that talking won't make the deadline disappear — but sometimes when we're under this much pressure, our thoughts can make the situation feel even more impossible than it actually is, and that's worth exploring. I'm curious, when you say the deadline "feels impossible," what's the thought that goes through your mind — is it more "I *might* struggle to finish this" or something closer to "there's absolutely no way this can be done"?

client: Honestly, it's closer to the second one — like, there's this voice in my head that just keeps saying "there's no way you're going to pull this off, you never do." It's not just about this one deadline, it's more like... evidence that I'm fundamentally not capable of handling things the way other people seem to. And when I try to tell myself "maybe it'll be okay," it just feels like lying to myself, so I don't even bother.
therapist: That voice sounds really harsh and exhausting to live with, and I want to acknowledge how painful it is when even trying to reassure yourself feels dishonest. What you're describing — that leap from "I'm struggling with this deadline" to "I'm fundamentally not capable" — is actually a very common cognitive pattern where one difficult situation gets used as proof of something much bigger about who you are. I'd gently ask you to consider: when you say you "never" pull things off, are there any moments, even small ones, that might not quite fit that story?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there have been times when I got things done, but it feels like those don't really count somehow, like they were flukes or I just got lucky. It's hard to hold onto those moments when the current situation feels so overwhelming and real. And honestly, part of me worries that if I start telling myself "see, you can do it," I'm just setting myself up to feel even worse when I fail again.
therapist: What you just did there is actually really significant — you found real evidence that contradicts that harsh inner voice, even if it immediately got dismissed as a "fluke," and that dismissal is worth paying attention to as a pattern in itself. It's like your mind has a rule where successes don't count but struggles count as proof of everything, which isn't a fair system and naturally makes that voice feel impossible to argue with. I'm wondering — what do you think would have to be true about one of those past successes for it to "count" as genuinely yours?

client: That's... actually a really uncomfortable question, because when I sit with it, I'm not sure anything would count. Like, even if I try to come up with conditions — "okay, if I did it completely alone, with no help, under pressure" — I can already feel my mind finding a way to add another condition on top of that. It's like the goalpost just keeps moving, and I think part of me knows that, but knowing it doesn't make it stop.
therapist: The fact that you can see the goalposts moving in real time, even while it's happening, is actually a really important insight — it suggests that part of you recognizes this isn't a fair evaluation of your capabilities, even if it doesn't feel that way emotionally yet. What you're describing sounds less like an honest assessment of your abilities and more like a system that's designed, perhaps without you choosing it, to make sure you never feel good enough. I'm curious — when you imagine where that rule might have come from, does anything come to mind?

client: Yeah, I mean... when I think about where it comes from, my dad immediately comes to mind. He was never really satisfied with anything I did — I'd get a good grade and he'd ask why it wasn't perfect, or I'd finish a project and he'd point out what was wrong with it before saying anything else. I guess I just internalized that voice and now I do it to myself without even needing him in the room.
therapist: That's a really profound and courageous connection to make — you essentially learned to see yourself through your father's eyes, and that critical voice became so familiar that it feels like *your* voice now, even though it was never really yours to begin with. It makes so much sense that reassuring yourself feels fake, because that inner critic was built to override exactly that kind of self-compassion. I'm wondering — if you imagine a close friend coming to you with the same struggles you're facing at work right now, would you apply that same impossible, ever-moving standard to them?

client: I mean... no, obviously I wouldn't talk to a friend that way. If a friend told me they were struggling to keep up at work, I'd probably just listen and tell them it makes sense given everything they're dealing with. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just feels like I'm making excuses, like I'm letting myself off the hook for something I should be able to handle.
therapist: You just named something really important — that the same compassion you'd freely offer a friend feels like a moral failure when you turn it toward yourself, which tells us that self-compassion has somehow gotten tangled up with the idea of being "weak" or "making excuses" in your mind. But I'd gently challenge that: when you listen to a friend and say "this makes sense given what you're dealing with," you're not letting them off the hook — you're actually helping them see their situation more clearly so they can move forward. What do you think it would feel like, even just as an experiment, to try offering yourself that same kind of honest, caring perspective for just one moment today?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it logically. But when I try to imagine doing that for myself, there's this immediate voice that says "yeah, but your friend actually deserves that kindness" — like I'm a special exception to the rule somehow. It feels less like an experiment and more like I'd be lying to myself, because some part of me genuinely believes I've made too many mistakes to deserve that kind of understanding.
therapist: That belief — that you've somehow accumulated too many mistakes to deserve basic kindness — is one of the most painful things a person can carry, and I want you to know that I hear how real and deeply held it feels. But I'd gently point out that you wouldn't tell your struggling friend "sorry, you've made too many mistakes to deserve understanding" — and the fact that you'd never apply that rule to someone else suggests it isn't actually a principle you believe in, but rather that original critical voice convincing you that *you specifically* are the exception. I'm curious — when you think about the "mistakes" that feel like they disqualify you, are those things you chose carelessly, or were they more often you doing your best under really difficult circumstances?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's not that simple. Like, some of those mistakes weren't me just "doing my best" — there were times I knew better and still made the wrong call, and I think that's what really gets to me. So when you say I'd never apply that rule to a friend, maybe that's because my friend didn't actually know better in the moment, but I did.
therapist: That distinction you're making actually shows a lot of moral seriousness and self-awareness, and I don't want to dismiss it — it matters to you to hold yourself accountable, and that's not nothing. But I'd gently ask: when a person knows better and still makes the wrong call, what does that usually mean — that they're fundamentally undeserving of understanding, or that they were human, perhaps overwhelmed or afraid or pulled in competing directions in that moment? What do you think you were really needing or trying to protect when you made those calls?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept it, but it still feels like a convenient excuse — like "I was overwhelmed" is just a way to let myself off the hook. When I pulled away from my friends during that period, I think I was trying to protect myself from feeling like a burden, but that doesn't change the fact that they needed me and I wasn't there. I guess I was scared that if I showed up as the mess I was, they'd see how much I was struggling and either pull away themselves or feel obligated to carry me.
therapist: What you just described — pulling away to protect your friends from your pain, at the cost of your own connection and support — actually sounds like an act of care, even if it was also an act of fear, and that's a really different thing than selfishness or not caring. You were a person in real pain, trying not to become a burden, and the cruel irony is that the same sensitivity that made you worry about them is now being used as evidence against you. I'm wondering — if one of those friends had pulled away from you during a hard time for exactly the same reason, would you feel like they had failed you, or would you feel sad that they didn't feel safe enough to let you in?

client: I sat with that for a second, and honestly... no, I wouldn't feel like they failed me. I'd feel sad, like you said, and I'd probably wish they'd trusted me enough to reach out. But it's still really hard to apply that same logic to myself, because somehow when it's me doing it, it just feels like I made excuses and let people down.
therapist: You just gave yourself the same answer twice — once for your friend, and once for yourself — and they were the same answer, even though every part of you wanted them to be different. That gap between what you *know* and what you *feel* about yourself is really the heart of what we've been exploring today, and it makes sense that it's hard to close, because that critical voice has had a lot more practice than this newer, more honest one. I'm wondering — what would it mean for you, even in a small way, if that voice that says "I let people down" wasn't the final word on who you are?
